title.en: Phases of the Moon (additional, not in the textbook)

text.en:
Anu watched the Moon every night for a month. On one night it was a bright round disc. A week later it was a half circle, and later it was a thin curve.
"Is someone eating the Moon?" she asked.
Her grandfather laughed. "No, we only see part of its lit side."

The Moon does not make its own light. It shines because sunlight falls on it. Always half of the Moon is lit by the Sun.
The Moon goes round the Earth in about one month. As it moves, we see different amounts of its lit half. These shapes are called phases of the Moon.
On the full moon night we see the whole lit face. On the new moon night we cannot see it. In between it looks like a crescent or a half moon. After the new moon the bright part grows, which is the waxing phase, and after the full moon it shrinks, which is the waning phase.
The Moon has no light of its own. It shines because the Sun lights it.
As the Moon goes round the Earth, we see different parts of its lit side.
These shapes are the phases. Full moon shows the whole lit face. On new moon we cannot see it.
The cycle of phases takes about one month.

problem.en: Why do we not see the Moon on a new moon night?

text.en: On a new moon the lit half faces away from us.

why.en: The lit side is turned away.

text.en: We see only the dark half, which cannot be seen in the dark sky.
A few days later a thin crescent appears.

prompt.en: A friend says the Moon changes shape because the Earth's shadow covers it. How will you explain?

requiredIdeas.en: Phases are caused by how much of the lit half we see as the Moon moves round the Earth.
The Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse, which is different.

points.en: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight.
We see different parts of the lit half: the phases.
The cycle takes about a month.
